text: The killing of the suitors is presented as just punishment, sanctioned by the gods. But its scale and violence, Odysseus' refusal to accept compensation, and the cruel deaths of Melanthius and the maids have troubled many readers. Some see the poem as endorsing the restoration of the master's authority over his household by any means [[thalmann1998]].

The maids have become a focus of feminist and social criticism. They are slaves, and their relations with the suitors may not have been freely chosen; their punishment is decided by Eurycleia and carried out by Telemachus. Critics have asked whether the poem invites any sympathy for them; the simile of the trapped birds suggests a note of pity [[doherty1995]] [[cohen1995]].

debates.title: The Telemachy
text: The first four books focus on Telemachus, and Odysseus does not appear until Book 5. Analysts argued that the Telemachy was originally an independent poem, later attached to the Odyssey, citing apparent inconsistencies, such as the abrupt shift of scene and the long absence of the hero [[page1955]].

Unitarians argue that the Telemachy is integral: it introduces the situation in Ithaca, shows the need for Odysseus' return, develops the theme of the son's growth, and builds suspense by delaying the hero's appearance. The parallel stories of Nestor, Menelaus and Agamemnon also frame Odysseus' return [[clay1983]] [[heubeck1988]] [[dejong2001]].

debates.title: The Odyssey and the Iliad: one poet or two?
text: Ancient scholars called chorizontes ('separators') argued that the two poems were by different poets; Aristarchus opposed them. 'Longinus' thought the Odyssey the work of Homer's old age. Modern scholars note differences in vocabulary, theology and social world, and many think the poems were composed by different poets, perhaps a generation apart [[graziosi2002]] [[west2014]].

Others argue for a single poet or tradition, noting the poems' shared style and the way the Odyssey seems to complement the Iliad, avoiding its episodes while engaging with its values. Gregory Nagy's model of a gradual crystallisation of the tradition makes the question of individual authorship less relevant [[nagy1979]] [[griffin1987]].

debates.title: Butler's 'authoress'
text: In The Authoress of the Odyssey (1897), the novelist Samuel Butler argued that the poem was composed by a young woman of Trapani in Sicily, who portrayed herself as Nausicaa. He based the argument on the poem's interest in domestic life, the prominence of its female characters and what he saw as a woman's errors about ships and male activities [[butler1897]].

The thesis has never been accepted by scholars, but it has been taken seriously as a provocation. Robert Graves made it the basis of his novel Homer's Daughter (1955), and later critics have used it to raise questions about gender, voice and audience in the poem [[hall2008]] [[doherty1995]].

quotes.quote: Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many devices, who wandered full many ways after he had sacked the sacred citadel of Troy.
quotes.explanation: The proem names its subject only as 'the man', without saying who he is, and defines him by his versatility (polytropos) and his wandering. The suppression of the name, which does not appear until line 21, anticipates the hero's disguises and the poem's concern with identity.

quotes.quote: Look you now, how ready mortals are to blame the gods. It is from us, they say, that evils come, but they even of themselves, through their own blind folly, have sorrows beyond that which is ordained.
quotes.explanation: Zeus' complaint, prompted by the story of Aegisthus, sets out the moral framework of the poem. Human beings are responsible for their own suffering, and those who ignore divine warnings will be punished, as the companions and the suitors will be.

quotes.quote: I will endure it, having in my breast a heart that endures affliction.
quotes.explanation: Odysseus' answer to Calypso's warning that he will suffer more on the voyage home. Endurance is his defining quality, and his decision to leave the goddess defines his choice of mortal life over immortality.

quotes.quote: For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord
quotes.explanation: Odysseus' wish for Nausicaa describes the marital harmony (homophrosynē) that is the poem's ideal, and that he and Penelope will demonstrate through the shared secret of the bed.

quotes.quote: Noman is my name, Noman do they call me
quotes.explanation: The false name tricks the Cyclops into telling his neighbours that 'Noman' is killing him. It also puns on mētis, cunning, and shows how Odysseus survives by giving up his identity, which he will dangerously reclaim at the end of the episode.

quotes.quote: I should choose, so I might live on earth, to serve as the hireling of another, of some portionless man whose livelihood was but small, rather than to be lord over all the dead that have perished.
quotes.explanation: In the underworld Achilles rejects Odysseus' consolation. His words seem to reverse the choice of glory over life that he made in the Iliad, and to endorse the Odyssey's values of survival and return.

quotes.quote: He spoke, and made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth
quotes.explanation: The narrator's comment on Odysseus' lies to Penelope. It recalls the Muses' boast in Hesiod's Theogony that they can tell lies like the truth, and identifies Odysseus as a poet of deception.

quotes.quote: Endure, my heart; a worse thing even than this didst thou once endure on that day when the Cyclops, unrestrained in daring, devoured my mighty comrades
quotes.explanation: Odysseus restrains his anger at the maids by recalling his patience in the Cyclops' cave. The self-address shows his mastery of himself and links his revenge to his earlier cunning.

quotes.quote: And welcome as is the sight of land to men that swim
quotes.explanation: The simile describing Penelope's joy at the reunion recalls Odysseus' own shipwreck, transferring his experience to her and suggesting the equality of their suffering.

quotes.quote: Therefore the fame of her virtue shall never perish, but the immortals shall make among men on earth a pleasant song in honor of constant Penelope.
quotes.explanation: Agamemnon's ghost praises Penelope's fidelity and contrasts her with Clytemnestra. The kleos usually won by warriors is here promised to a woman for her constancy.

questions.q: Why does the Odyssey begin with Telemachus rather than Odysseus?
questions.hint: Think about how the Telemachy establishes the situation in Ithaca, creates suspense and presents the theme of the son's growing up. Consider the effect of meeting Odysseus first through other people's memories.

questions.q: Is Odysseus a reliable narrator of his own adventures?
questions.hint: Consider his audience and purposes among the Phaeacians, his false tales in Ithaca, and the narrator's comment in Book 19. Does the poem give us reasons to trust or doubt the Apologue?

questions.q: How does the Odyssey define heroism differently from the Iliad?
questions.hint: Compare Odysseus' qualities with Achilles'. Consider Achilles' words in the underworld, Odysseus' choice of mortality, and the poem's emphasis on endurance and cunning.

questions.q: How far does Penelope know or suspect the beggar's identity before Book 23?
questions.hint: Look closely at Books 18 and 19, especially her dream and her decision to set the contest. Weigh the narrator's statements against the hints and ambiguities.

questions.q: What role does hospitality play in the moral structure of the poem?
questions.hint: Compare the scenes at Pylos, Sparta, Scheria and Eumaeus' hut with the Cyclops and the suitors. How is xenia linked to divine justice?

questions.q: Is the killing of the suitors and the maids just?
questions.hint: Consider the warnings the suitors receive, the refusal of compensation, the treatment of Amphinomus, Melanthius and the maids, and the need for divine intervention at the end.

questions.q: What is the significance of the recognition tokens: the scar, the bow, the bed and the trees?
questions.hint: Think about how each connects identity to the body, to skill, to marriage or to family history, and why different tokens suit different people.

questions.q: How does the poem portray women and their power?
questions.hint: Consider Penelope, Helen, Arete, Nausicaa, Calypso, Circe, Eurycleia and the maids. Do the female characters share any common qualities or functions?

questions.q: What does the Odyssey suggest about the power and dangers of song and storytelling?
questions.hint: Think about Phemius, Demodocus, the Sirens and Odysseus as storyteller. Consider the pleasure, grief and deception that song can produce.

questions.q: Does Book 24 provide a satisfying ending to the poem?
questions.hint: Weigh the arguments that the poem ends at 23.296 against the case for Book 24. Consider the reunion with Laertes, the second visit to the underworld, and Athena's imposed peace.
